# How to Make an Animated Cartoon of Yourself with Picsart Flow

> **In short:** Picsart's "Flow" template turns a single portrait photo into a full-body cartoon character and then animates it, all inside one editor. You upload, pick the template, let it run, and download — no design skills required.

You've got a headshot on your phone and ten minutes to spare. By the end of this guide, that headshot will be a moving cartoon character — walking, blinking, doing whatever the template decides. It's a fun weekend project, and once you've done it once, you'll understand how these "image-to-video" tools work in general.

## What Picsart Flow actually does

Picsart is a phone and web editor (think Photoshop, but friendlier, made for non-designers). **Flow** is their name for a series of ready-made AI templates — little one-click workflows that bundle several AI steps together. The cartoon-selfie template bundles two:

1. **Image generation** — the AI reads your face from the photo and draws you as a full-body cartoon character in a chosen style. (Image generation means the AI creates a brand-new picture based on your photo, rather than editing the photo itself.)
2. **Image-to-video animation** — the AI takes that new cartoon picture and adds motion: a few seconds of walking, looking around, hair moving, that kind of thing. (Image-to-video means starting with a still picture and producing a short video from it.)

Both steps sit inside the same editor on the same canvas, so you can preview and re-run each one without leaving the screen.

## What you'll need before you start

Before you tap anything, get these in place — it'll save you the frustration of getting halfway through and realizing you're missing something.

- **A Picsart account.** Free works. You can sign in with email, Google, or Apple.
- **The Picsart mobile app** (iOS or Android) or the web editor at picsart.com. The mobile app tends to be smoother for this template.
- **One clear, well-lit photo of a face.** Front-facing, no sunglasses, no heavy hat, eyes visible. The better the input, the more the cartoon actually looks like you.
- **A paid Picsart subscription** for the highest quality output and watermark-free downloads. The free tier lets you try the template, but the final export usually has a Picsart watermark (a small logo stamped on the image) and a lower resolution. The exact plan name and price change often — check Picsart's official pricing page for current details.

Got all that? Good. Let's go.

## Step 1 — Open the template in the editor

Open the Picsart app, tap the **plus (+)** button at the bottom of the screen to start a new project, then look for **"AI Tools"** or **"Flow"** in the menu. Search for the template called something like **"Cartoon yourself"** or **"AI portrait animation."**

When you tap it, the editor will open with a single big canvas (your workspace — the main editing area in the middle of the screen) and a panel on the side that lists the two steps in order. You'll see a button to upload your photo.

💬 **Tip:** use a photo where your face takes up most of the frame, with even lighting and a simple background. Busy backgrounds confuse the AI and you'll get stranger results.

**You'll know it worked when** you see your uploaded photo appear on the canvas and the first step — the image generation step — is highlighted as "ready to run."

## Step 2 — Run the cartoon generation

Tap the **"Generate"** or **"Run"** button for the first step. The AI will think for about 20 to 60 seconds — during this time it's analyzing your face and redrawing it as a cartoon character. You'll see a progress bar or a loading spinner.

When it finishes, the canvas will show your new cartoon version next to the original photo so you can compare. Most templates let you re-run it several times to get different results — each run produces a slightly different cartoon.

💬 **If you want a different look**, look for a "style" or "vibe" selector (often a row of small preview thumbnails at the bottom of the screen). Try a few before you move on. Anime, comic-book, and 3D-toon styles are common options.

**You'll know it worked when** you see a recognizable cartoon character on the canvas that clearly resembles you, with a full body and a background.

## Step 3 — Add motion to the cartoon

Now look at the second step in the side panel — usually labeled **"Animate"** or **"Add motion."** Tap it. You'll typically get a few motion options: subtle movement (blinking, hair sway, breathing) or full-body movement (walking, turning, dancing).

Pick one and tap **"Generate."** This step takes longer — anywhere from one to five minutes, depending on server load (how many other people are using Picsart at the same time).

💬 **Suggestion:** start with the subtle movement. It's faster, looks more natural, and is less likely to glitch. Save the dramatic walking-and-waving version for your second try.

**You'll know it worked when** a short video preview appears in the canvas, and you can press play to see your cartoon character moving.

## Step 4 — Preview and tweak

Watch the preview all the way through. Look for three common problems:

- The face doesn't look like you.
- The motion has weird artifacts (visible glitches — for example, fingers that melt together, a background that warps, or limbs that bend the wrong way).
- The style isn't what you wanted.

If any of these happen, just re-run whichever step produced the problem. You can re-run step 2 to get a new cartoon, or re-run step 3 to get a new animation. Nothing is final until you export.

## Step 5 — Export and save

When you're happy with the result, tap the **"Export"** or **"Download"** button — usually in the top-right corner. The app will ask whether you want a still image (the cartoon) or a video (the animation). Pick the video to get both the moving character and a watermark-free version of the cartoon frame.

💬 **File format tip:** MP4 is the safest format for sharing on social media and messaging apps. Stick with the default unless you have a specific reason to change it.

**You'll know it worked when** the file appears in your phone's photo library or downloads folder, and you can play it back without the Picsart editor around it.

## Common mistakes to avoid

- **Using a group photo.** The AI needs one face. With several faces, it'll guess wrong or merge features.
- **Wearing sunglasses or a face mask.** The AI can't see your eyes or mouth, and the cartoon will look generic.
- **Skipping the re-run step.** Your first cartoon is rarely the best one. Run it three or four times and pick your favorite.
- **Picking a motion that's too dramatic.** Long walking animations on a single still image are where you see the most weird artifacts. Subtle motion is more forgiving.
- **Forgetting to check the watermark situation.** On a free plan, your video will have a small Picsart logo. If that bothers you, look at the paid plans before you share publicly.

## What this means for you

- **If you just want a fun profile picture:** Run only step 2 (the cartoon), skip the animation, and you've got a unique avatar (a small picture that represents you online) in about a minute. The animated version is the bonus.
- **If you're a small business owner or creator:** This kind of template is a fast, low-cost way to make branded characters for social posts, story reactions, or short video clips — without hiring an illustrator.
- **If you're worried about AI and likeness:** You're uploading a photo of *yourself*, so you stay in control. The cartoon is a stylized version of you, not a deepfake (a fake video that pretends to be a real person saying or doing things they never did) of someone else. The tool isn't scanning your face for any hidden purpose.
- **If you're just curious about AI image tools:** This is a gentle on-ramp. The same two-step pattern — "turn a photo into a stylized image, then animate it" — shows up in dozens of creative tools right now. Once you've done it here, the others will feel familiar.

## Wrap-up

You started with one photo. You ended with a short animated video of yourself as a cartoon character, made in roughly five to ten minutes, with no design skills. That's the real story here: a class of AI tools that used to require a professional illustrator and a video editor is now a one-tap template in a phone app. Try the subtle-movement version first, re-run the steps a few times until you like the result, and post it somewhere fun. Your next experiment could be the same template on a pet photo — it works for animals too.
